title: Where neighbors ask for review: tracts by income and residents
question: Do requests for discretionary review come more often from tracts with higher incomes and more white residents, as the neighborhood figures suggested?
finding: Per 100,000 households, 18 review requests came from the lowest-income third of tracts and 106 from the highest (+0.38 across 232 tracts: a weak link, beyond what chance would produce); 18 from the third with the fewest white residents and 120 from the third with the most (+0.41 across 237 tracts: a moderate link, beyond what chance would produce). Against the neighborhood-level links in the planning-applications screen (0.61 with income, 0.63 with the white share), at tract level the link with income holds and the link with the white share holds.
how: Each discretionary-review case number in the Planning Commission minutes is counted once and placed in a 2020 census tract by parcel or address. All tracts with 500 or more residents are ranked by each Census measure and cut into thirds; the rate is requests per 100,000 households in the third. The rank correlation is across all those tracts, most of which have no request.
limits: AREA LEVEL ONLY. A review is a review of a permit, so requests can only arise where permits are filed: if permits for additions to houses are concentrated in owner-occupied, higher-income tracts, the pattern is about where such permits are filed, not about who objects. The planning-applications screen divided by permits; this one divides by households because permits by tract are not in these files. The minutes list requests that reached the calendar in 2019-2022, not all requests filed, and do not print who asked. A difference between areas, or between groups of cases, is not proof of bias. Areas differ in what is proposed, in zoning, lot sizes, building ages and land prices, and in who chooses to apply, object or appeal at all.
